name: Bhutan
summary: A Himalayan Buddhist kingdom unified by Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal from 1616; ruled by the Wangchuck kings since 1907; measures “Gross National Happiness”.

terrain.value: Himalayan mountains in the north rise from subtropical plains in the south; fast rivers have carved deep gorges.

climate.value: Varies with height: subtropical in the south, temperate in the highlands and year-round snow in the north.

resources.value: One of the world's largest water reserves for hydropower; forests covered 64% of the land in 2005.

disasters.value: Glacial floods, made worse by melting glaciers; Japan is helping build an early warning system.

urbanisation.value: Thimphu, the capital and largest city, holds close to 15% of the population.

disease.value: Basic healthcare is free under the constitution; life expectancy was 70.2 years in 2016.

migration.value: From the 1980s to the early 1990s, 80,000–100,000 Nepali-speaking Lhotshampa were deported and became refugees in Nepal; many later resettled in Western countries.

economicBase.value: Exports are mainly electricity, plus cardamom, gypsum and timber; tourism is also important.

tradeRoutes.value: A 2008 free-trade accord with India lets Bhutan's trade pass through India without tariffs.

moneyAndTax.value: The ngultrum, fixed to the Indian rupee.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: A democratic constitutional monarchy; the 2008 Constitution set up a parliamentary government.

keyRulers.value: Ngawang Namgyal. Ugyen Wangchuck. Jigme Singye Wangchuck.

succession.value: Hereditary kings of the Wangchuck dynasty since Ugyen Wangchuck was chosen in 1907.

institutions.value: The 2008 Constitution created a parliament with an elected National Assembly and a National Council.

eliteConflict.value: In the 1870s rivalry between the valleys of Paro and Tongsa led to civil war.

armyAndTech.value: A small army trained by India; there is no navy or air force.

territoryChange.value: Ceded the Bengal Duars to British India after losing the Duar War (Treaty of Sinchula).

alliancesRivals.value: Close to India, which helps with defence and funds a quarter of the budget.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: Education was traditionally monastic; secular schooling for everyone began in the 1960s.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: Paro Airport is the only international airport.

religion.value: Vajrayana Buddhism (the state religion) is followed by two-thirds to three-quarters of people; Hinduism by 22.6%.

languageWriting.value: Dzongkha is the national language, written in a form of Tibetan script; English is used in schools.

artsArchitecture.value: Dzongs (fortresses) that are still centres of religion and government; the Mask dance of the drums from Drametse is UNESCO-listed.

socialStructure.value: Mainly Ngalops (western) and Sharchops (eastern), plus Nepali-speaking Lhotshampa in the south.

sharedIdentity.value: Officially Druk Yul, "Land of the Thunder Dragon"; government employees must wear the national dress.

dailyLife.value: Red rice, buckwheat and maize are staples; ema datshi (chilies and cheese) is the national dish.

ideasReligions.value: The Drukpa Lineage of Vajrayana Buddhism, the country's dominant sect.

colonisation.value: Never officially colonised, though effectively a British protectorate after the 1910 Treaty of Punakha.

riseSignals.value: Unified into a single state by Ngawang Namgyal in the early 17th century.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
